claims.text: The target alloy is a Co-free FeNiCrMn derivative of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
The initial FeNiCrMn alloy is a solidified solid solution with a random chemical distribution.
The temperature- and strain-rate-dependent dynamic response of FeNiCrMn is controlled by a strain-induced short-range-ordering transition.
High-strain-rate compression at low-to-moderate temperatures drives a clustering-to-ordering transition.
The compression-induced ordered state has increased unlike-atom pair correlations and decreased clustering.
Severe deformation produces local atomic rearrangements that favor unlike atomic neighbors.
Short-range ordering creates additional obstacles to dislocation motion.
The ordering-induced obstacles raise flow stress.
The proposed ordering enhances ductility through dynamic strain hardening.
Tensile loading does not produce the clustering-to-ordering transition and leaves the alloy clustering-dominated.
The tensile baseline has lower flow stress and less dynamic strain hardening than compression under otherwise identical conditions.
Elevated temperature suppresses ordering through thermal agitation and reduces strain hardening.
Compression at high strain rate and low-to-moderate temperature will produce statistically higher flow stress and strain hardening than tension.
Structural measurements will show greater unlike-pair short-range order after or during compression than during tension.
The proposed mechanism is most relevant below approximately 700 K.
A sufficiently high strain rate is required to drive the proposed nonequilibrium atomic rearrangements.
Very high temperatures or very low strain rates may prevent significant short-range order from forming.
Failure of compression to produce both higher mechanical response and greater unlike-pair ordering than the matched tensile control would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis distinguishes a clustering-dominated state from an unlike-pair ordered state, but the structural mediator calls unlike-atom association 'clustering (ordering),' conflating the two states and making the mediator terminology internally inconsistent.
